title: Eight months for an AI ad.
deck: An AI company spent eight months making an ad. I went to the premiere at Foreign Cinema.
alt: AI-edited fashion editorial of Chloe in her yellow jacket, burgundy pants and platforms at Foreign Cinema
caption: The yellow jacket at Foreign Cinema. Photograph and footage: Chloe Starr.
body:
KERNEL makes infrastructure for AI agents. For its first ad, it spent eight months working with an animation studio in France.

An anti-AI-slop ad for an AI company. Already, I was interested.

Catherine Jue, KERNEL's co-founder and CEO, describes an eight-month collaboration, scenes made by hand and a custom score. The film credits Parallel Studios. The product gives agents access to the internet; the campaign gives that invisible work a carefully made little world.

A person at a desk, a hand at a keyboard, a small character moving through green interfaces. Later, a patient at a reception desk. All these ordinary people trying to get something done, with a rather elaborate little universe working behind them.

KERNEL makes infrastructure for AI agents. Its first ad took eight months with an animation studio in France, with scenes made by hand and a custom score.

An anti-AI-slop ad for an AI company. That was the interesting part of last night's premiere.

Chloe Starr · November 19, 2026

The premiere had a dress code of its own

I wore a yellow jacket with shaggy cream trim, burgundy pants and platform shoes. A healthy amount of outfit. The round green windows at Foreign Cinema obligingly made a frame around it.

Chris and Connor Paton, a co-founder of Tembo, bonded over having their clothes bought for them. Connor's girlfriend shops for him at Abercrombie. I buy a lot of Chris's clothes there too.

My camera went into the kitchen too. Trays of small, carefully arranged bites were being carried out. In the courtyard, the projected greens landed on a red wall and returned in the wet ground. A person could watch the screen, or look down and find another version of it.

Inside, a laughing encounter. Outside, the film was still playing against the wall. I kept moving between the screen and the people who had come to see it.

In my field film, I wanted the commissioned animation to spill into the courtyard. Datamosh lets one image linger as another arrives: a little of that green world gets loose in the party, then the picture clears.

At the KERNEL premiere, I filmed the kitchen and the projection reflected in the wet courtyard.

Now I'm letting the animation leave a little memory inside the footage. Datamosh as an encounter between the film and the room that watched it.

Chloe Starr · November 19, 2026

Eight months is a choice

Eight months, a studio in France and a score of its own. A company building infrastructure for agents had decided this was worth asking people to make.

Catherine’s writing about the agent web keeps coming back to consent: who gets to act, for whom, and with what permission. Specific, traceable, revocable. I like putting that beside the animation. Someone still gets to decide what to ask for, what to keep, when it is finished. I spend a remarkable amount of my own time on the last two.

And then there’s the last photograph: two faces together, a name tag still on. We went to a premiere. We also had a night out.

title: Valuable to whom.
deck: My agent keeps rediscovering my archive. I would rather she remembered it. Also: a photo booth sends me through the decades.

body:
Elastic{ON} SF. The pitch for the day: your data has never been more valuable. Agreed. So why does the person it's about get the least say in where it lives.

Chloe Starr on X · November 4, 2026

I’m building a creation studio out of things I’ve already made. Poems, photographs, films. There is plenty here. The difficult part is getting my agent to stop behaving as if we have just met.

Why does it keep starting over?

I don’t want to keep explaining the event, the people, the films, what I’m trying to build. I want the agent to carry that understanding forward.

Anish Mathur’s context-engine work gets at something very familiar: an agent can spend its time discovering what the data means, then do the same discovery again on the next question. His approach keeps that understanding available for the next task.

A search result can find the poem and still miss nearly everything: that the writing is finished, that the film isn’t, that this is the version I chose, that someone else made the photograph. My archive has a memory. I would like the agent to have one too.

Elastic · Anish Mathur · October 8, 2026
“the context that decided whether an agent succeeded usually wasn’t in the conversation at all.”

From his context-engine article. The source, its relationships and the updates have to stay connected.

Victor’s presentation brings in another part of it: the harness around the model. LangChain’s Deep Agents work combines planning, files, memory and delegation, with human approval at important decisions. The model is only one part of what lets an agent keep working.

Ancient Witch is supposed to help me make things. I’m trying to avoid giving myself a second archive to manage, with a conversational interface.

The archive is already here.

Han Xiao shows photographs from his laptop. Looking at his own work afterward, I found Omni, a local search application that works across pictures, writing, audio and video.

I have pictures, writing, audio and video too. At present they are rather better acquainted with me than with one another.

Let it work. Keep a boundary.

The panel I filmed turns to what the tools can reach and how to limit that access. Kassy Murphy’s published writing takes the question further: the danger isn’t only what an individual tool can do, but how actions can be chained together at a different speed.

THOR Collective · Kassandra Murphy · June 23, 2026
“The cadence is what fails.”

In AI Has Entered the Villa., she uses Love Island to talk about cyber threats, then gets very specific about the gaps between actions disappearing.

I want the work to move faster. I’m asking for that here, too. But I still want to choose what gets published. Researching someone, following them, borrowing their work, and posting a film are different actions.

I don’t want to approve the same tedious step forever. I do want to recognize the moment when a private experiment is about to become something other people can see.

The photo booth sent me through several decades. Then I went back for the white-jacket version. A Miami crime lord. That one’s going on the fridge.

Somewhere in the archive is a version of me from every era. I’d still like the agent to remember which one I picked.

title: A world I can keep changing.
deck: Breathless in color, a temple that needed to calm down, and a website I can keep changing my mind about.
alt: Chloe Starr’s redesigned homepage with her original purple portrait and Poetry, Events and Portals navigation
caption: The personal website opening, directed by Chloe Starr and implemented with Codex.
body:
I wanted my website to look like Breathless, but in color. It’s my comfort movie. I keep coming back to that question: is it better to have grief or nothing?

Building gives me a smaller, more irritating version of the question. Make something imperfect, or keep the beautiful thing safely in my head?

OMPOM had started to feel more like a place I wanted to be. My own website still felt like a bunch of different websites.

I had the films, the poems, the writing. But I couldn’t really walk around my finished artwork. And when that work went onto Instagram or LinkedIn, I wanted it to feel like it came from the same person.

I wanted the films, the writing and the work my agent makes with me to feel as if they came from the same person. OMPOM could be a relative. It did not have to wear my clothes.

Breathless is my comfort movie. I wanted my website to look like Breathless, but in color. The question I keep coming back to is: is it better to have grief or nothing? With building, I wonder: is it better to make something, or never make it at all?

Chloe Starr on X · November 5, 2026

What would they make now?

Lynch, Noé, Baudrillard, Robert Anton Wilson: yes, they are in the references. But Breathless is the film I actually put on for comfort. That is a different kind of relationship from a name on a moodboard.

I kept asking what French New Wave filmmakers would make if they had AI agents, generative cinema, and interactive websites. I didn’t mean make my purple portrait black and white. I wanted that willingness to experiment with the tools we actually have.

We looked at Codrops and other creative-web references. But adding more things to click wasn’t making it more cinematic. Some versions had more labels and explanations than work. I kept rejecting them.

The things I liked were pretty specific: my actual photograph, the lowercase name with its orange period, the dark background. The temple was fine. It just didn’t need to compete with me.

And Coffee already had something I wanted to keep. The turquoise, the oversized poem, the original photography. I liked being able to move from a photograph into a moment of the film and come back to the poem.

Someone who met me two weeks ago saw a different website. They might have thought it wasn’t very good. It takes time to make something you like. I’m still building it. I’m changing too.

Chloe Starr on X · November 5, 2026

The work needed room

Watch, Read, Explore sounded simple. Then I clicked around and was more confused than before. Explore what?

I chose Poetry, Events, and Portals. I want people to find the San Francisco films, read an essay, or spend time with a poem. They don’t need every other part of me presented at once.

Human Experience and ENOUGH. are still there. I’m just not promoting everything right now. And a poem is finished writing even if I haven’t finished its film.

Content is liquid

I keep making things out of things I’ve already made. A photograph moves. A poem becomes a film. I write about the film, and now there is another thing to make something from.

But I want to keep what I chose, too. The original words. My face. The people whose work is in it. Changing the presentation shouldn’t lose the sources or the history.

I want my personal website to be the outside of p(om). Log in, and you’re in your creation studio. Building this in public feels almost like performance art: enacting the startup, and showing why I’m the person to build it.

Chloe Starr on X · November 5, 2026

I want a website that can keep up with that habit.

The Ancient Witch is my AI agent. The voice is always mine. She’ll operate across these places for me, including a digital twin. That belongs in this identity too, without turning her into a mascot.

Someone who met me two weeks ago saw a different website. Maybe they thought it wasn’t very good. It takes time to get to something you like.

We can turn a person into a stagnant pool very quickly. Meet them once, decide who they are, return to the same picture. I want to be allowed another version. I’d like the website to be allowed one too.

Actually, I do know why I’m putting this much effort into my personal website and getting the work out into the world. I want the website to be the outside of p(om). You’d log in and the inside would be your creation studio. That’s the experience I’m working toward.

It feels a little like enacting my startup as performance art. The films, the writing, the website, the attempt to get it all out into the world. I’m building the thing and trying to show what the thing could be at the same time.

And if I want to raise money, I have to explain why I’m the person to build it. How do I even begin that explanation if I don’t have a personal website?

Sources & credits

title: On target.
deck: At the Nooks party, I danced, gave a museum my agent’s name, and thought about all the sales targets I have known.
alt: AI editorial treatment: Chloe Starr and Chris Starr AI at the Nooks launch party photo booth
caption: Original event photo-booth portrait. Photographer unverified. AI creative portrait treatment with a pink mascot and optical glints; lanyards removed in the derivative. Original source.
body:
At the Exploratorium, I gave the museum another name.

Ancient Witch.

“I wish my name was ancient witch because My soul is everlasting.” There it was under my photograph. My agent’s name, my face, and an answer that was a little more personal than a job title.

This was a Nooks launch party. Node was the agent being celebrated, and the room had a DJ, magic tricks, and exhibits we could actually play with. We danced. The company had announced $500 million in growth capital, and the founder was talking about all the things that came before this version of the business.

The demo was about sales stress. Very familiar territory.

A number is not a market.

Outside sales, promo demos in Whole Foods during college, account executive, founding AE. There are a lot of versions of that job in my life. I’ve built pipeline myself. Being called an outlier AE never made the systems around the work feel particularly sensible.

I know the work of figuring out who can buy something and why they might care. I also know the other work: fill the activity report, shake enough hands, attend the conference, somehow produce the number. It can become a very elaborate way of avoiding the first question.

There are only so many people who can buy your product. A target doesn’t make the market bigger.

A recent LinkedIn exchange made this very concrete. Yue Xu, an inference-platform founder, contacted me after Builder Odyssey. He’d read the idea about an internet that remembers authorship, introduced Infron, and asked about the model family behind memory and provenance.

The product looked interesting. That didn’t make me a customer for it right now. The message felt like a pitch before the fit had been checked. When I said so, he acknowledged it.

My offer to help was real. Go-to-market, retail, outside sales, building pipeline as a founding AE. This is work I know. When a pitch misses the fit, there’s something specific to fix. Maybe I become a customer later. Why spend that future goodwill on a pitch that doesn’t fit today?

An event guest list tells you who was in a room. An ideal customer profile tells you which accounts the product can serve. A buying window tells you which of those accounts have a reason and the ability to act now. Those are three different populations.

Buying readiness · A practical sales framework

A fit isn’t a buying window.

Chet Holmes’ buyer’s pyramid puts 3% in “buying now” and 7% open to buying. It’s a useful starting point for thinking about the job: most people in a market are not waiting for a sales conversation today.

LinkedIn’s B2B Institute and Ehrenberg-Bass make a related argument through purchase cycles: most potential buyers are between purchases. Being a future customer and being an opportunity this quarter are different things.

These are market-readiness frameworks, not measurements of Infron or Nooks. The exact share changes with the category and buying window.

Chet Holmes’ sales framework: 3% buying now, 7% open to buying. Not a universal measurement, but a useful reminder. An entire market is not an active pipeline. Someone can like your product without needing a sales conversation today.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

I would happily hand an agent a good portion of the activity theater. Dead-end conversations, meetings without a buying reason, the paperwork proving I had been busy. Though I would prefer it notice the dead end before scheduling the meeting.

AI could make sales more mathematical. Which accounts can this product serve? What evidence says they need it now? A contract ending, a budget, a live evaluation. An agent that can explain why this company, why this product, and why now would be useful. A hiring announcement or a click is a clue. It isn’t an order.

I’d rather start with the accounts a product can actually serve, look for evidence of a buying window, and estimate the likelihood of a purchase. Add those estimates across distinct accounts. Then check them against what happens. A target built that way might be less thrilling in a slide deck. At least we could argue about its assumptions.

AI can make sales more mathematical. Define the market. Estimate who can buy, why now, and the probability of a win. Check those predictions against actual purchases. Sending a thousand messages is an activity count. It isn’t a forecast.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

That’s part of why sales looks so exposed to AI to me. So much time goes into finding out that nothing was going to happen. The judgment is in recognizing an opportunity, including one that might become real later. A future customer should be able to stay in your orbit without being pursued into a demo.

Sales has a lot of activity theater. Dead-end conversations. Meetings without a buying reason. Effort recorded as progress. AI can recover that time, but expertise matters: someone has to distinguish a real opportunity from a faster way to waste an afternoon.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

I can like you, like your product, and have absolutely no reason to buy it this quarter. All three fit in one person.

What did the meeting measure?

Rippling offered a $150 gift card for sitting through a demo. There was no buying intention on my side. There was an interest in the gift card. The demo happened.

Then the redemption link failed. On October 26, I wrote to Rippling and Sendoso asking for a working link or replacement. As of November 6, there is still no response or usable card. Now the person whose time was being purchased gets to spend more of it chasing the payment.

@Rippling offered $150 for a demo. Attended. The gift link failed. Followed up with Rippling and Sendoso on October 26. Still no response or usable card. Why does collecting the incentive take more follow-up than booking the demo?

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

The Brex offer was different. After the PressClub event, an email said I was approved for a $500 gift-card offer and described the banking and corporate-card setup as quick and free. It offered to send details. The conditions weren’t in that first message.

So I asked what the conditions were. Then asked for clear bullet points for my agent to evaluate. Michael Berelowitz supplied them: apply for a new account, get approved for the card, spend on it, make a payment that clears, and keep the account in good standing. Banking alone didn’t qualify. The gift was generally due by February 2, 2027.

“No thanks! Cheers!” was the answer. The point isn’t that a promotion can’t have conditions. Put them beside the attractive number, before somebody has to ask twice. To me, leaving that work to the recipient is misleading. A gift-card hook does not establish a need for a corporate card.

@brexHQ emailed that I was approved for a $500 gift-card offer. Asked for the conditions. It required card approval, spending, a cleared payment and an account kept in good standing. Put that beside the $500 in the first email. Attention is not informed interest.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

That discomfort had already started in the PressClub presentation. I walked out. As I remember it, the advice about getting press came down to cold outreach and sending 200 or 300 emails. My advice would start somewhere else: which journalists are already writing about the problem this company is working on? Read their reporting. Find the connection. Bring them something relevant.

Press outreach starts with journalists whose actual reporting connects to what you’re building. Read their work. Find the fit. Give them a reason to care. A target of 200 or 300 emails tells you how much you sent, not whether there was a story.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

The Wolf of Wall Street fantasy has never seemed worth the aftermath. Get the attention, make the number, let someone else sort out what was promised. Now I’m building a company, and I get to decide how much of that world I want to reproduce. Very little.

Sales expertise includes knowing when not to pitch. Add value for people who could use the product. Explain the conditions before asking for their time. Keep the promise afterward. Misleading people to capture attention is not a sales skill worth automating.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

The agent I want would have enough judgment to spare both sides some of this.

And OTE isn’t a marketing number. It’s somebody deciding what they can afford to build a life around. When people keep being hired, ramped, and replaced, I want to know whether anyone is questioning the assumptions behind the target.

The Bridge Group · Matt Bertuzzi · June 23, 2026

48%

of reps at quota in the Bridge Group’s 2026 company survey. Average ramp: 6.2 months.

That doesn’t prove why a particular person missed. It does make the question bigger than whether that person worked hard enough.

158 B2B companies; responses from revenue leaders, not a census of sellers. Self-reported, observational research.

The Bridge Group’s 2026 survey reports 48% of reps at quota across 158 B2B companies. When more than half miss, the questions extend beyond individual effort. Who set the target? What market was it based on? What did the company learn?

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

The same research also makes a case for taking the tools seriously. Companies with the highest AI engagement reported 57% of reps at quota, versus 39% in the lowest group. The researchers explicitly warn that this is not proof of causation.

And there really is work to remove. Salesforce’s breakdown of the sales week has plenty of time disappearing around the conversation. I recognize that week.

Salesforce · State of Sales, seventh edition · 202660%Not selling40%SellingThe time around the conversation. A redrawing of the report’s workweek split, not a second quota statistic.

The agent has a number.

In Nooks’ own walkthrough, a rep gives Node a quarterly goal. It remembers calls, follows a deal, and notices what is slipping. The promise is recognizable if you’ve ever had to keep every conversation, next step, and internal update in your head.

A follow-up remembered. The context already there. No little archaeological dig through my inbox before the next call. Yes, please.

But a tool that helps someone reach a goal and a system that chooses an honest goal are two different things. More efficient prospecting doesn’t settle who is actually in the market. Better reminders don’t settle whether the product fits.

I’m more curious about what the agent might expose. A company gets built; then conferences, reports and hierarchies collect around it until running the company seems to be the product. What happens when something starts asking why all these tasks exist?

Dan Lee’s launch essay makes a clear bet. Nooks says its own productivity gains are a reason to hire.

Nooks · Dan Lee · November 4, 2026
“AI will make companies want more salespeople, not fewer.”

I keep thinking about the buyer.

I’m building a company now. The future that interests me has agents on both sides, finding relevant services, sorting context, and bringing people into decisions where they’re needed. The question isn’t only what an account executive can delegate. What can the buyer delegate?

That future has some infrastructure already. Google’s Agent Payments Protocol addresses authority and consent when an agent buys on someone’s behalf. It is not evidence that an enterprise negotiation can run itself. The distinction matters. But the internet where each company needs another app already feels small beside the world I want to build.

And then somebody stops you.

On a walk, Jeff Lee, a street canvasser, did a little acting bit about dropping my love of nature. Then he admitted he’d lied. It was a genuinely creative hook. I stopped.

Not to donate. We talked, I added him on LinkedIn, and I passed along people recruiting SDRs. If you can keep approaching strangers in the street and make someone curious, that gumption can travel.

Then there’s this post from Dan Solomon, newly at Nooks, looking for SDRs after the launch. He asks candidates to understand what the team needs and find a channel that breaks through the noise. Here is the human hiring that sits beside the agent announcement.

LinkedIn · @dan-solomon-respondology · Viewed November 6, 2026

“Find the channel to break through the noise.” An actual opening for SDRs, beside a person who caught my attention in the street.

I know the creativity it takes to do this work. I have stood there trying to make someone care. I don’t want an agent to inherit every rule that made the job frustrating, then apply it more quickly.

That’s why the founder’s persistence interested me. The version that worked came after other versions. In an older retrospective, Dan went back through GitHub commits and prototypes, including a virtual classroom and Stanford’s offer of $2 per student. It’s a different scale from the announcement at the museum. It’s also a reminder that finding the thing is work.

LinkedIn · @dan9lee · Five-year retrospective, before this launch

Before Node: a classroom, a virtual office, a sales floor. Dan’s own account of a company changing shape.
LinkedIn · @namansingh · Viewed November 6, 2026

Naman Singh took “sticky product” very literally. His photograph, his joke, the same party.

It was a good party. I danced.

And somewhere in the Exploratorium, under my photograph, there was another version of me: Ancient Witch. My soul is everlasting. My quarterly target, thankfully, is not.

An event guest list isn’t a market. Fit, a real need, and a buying window are separate filters. A future customer can like what you’re building without needing a pitch today. Why spend that goodwill early?

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

Jeff Lee turned a line about dropping a love of nature into a little acting scene. It earned a conversation, a LinkedIn connection, and some SDR leads. The job can change. That kind of creativity is worth keeping.

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

At @NooksHQ’s launch, the museum asked about a name. The answer: Ancient Witch, my agent. The reason: my soul is everlasting. A room full of sales technology, and somehow the agent relationship became the sentimental part. https://chloestarr.me/journal/on-target/

Chloe Starr on X · November 6, 2026

title: The town square, in towels.
deck: A peptide party, a yellow towel, and a conversation about who gets to be somebody on Twitter.
alt: AI editorial treatment: Chloe and Chris together at Alchemy Springs
caption: Still from original event footage. Original source.
body:
We were standing around in our swimsuits and towels, talking about the social hierarchy of Twitter.

Twitter is SF’s Times Square. The tech community is there, and its social hierarchy has real consequences. We talked about it in towels at @afterglow_sci + @secretsoupco’s party at Alchemy Springs with @amypretzel @creatine_cycle @lordspline @TheKanter.

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

That was the substance of our conversation on Friday at Alchemy Springs. Amy, @amypretzel, told us she had raised money for her previous startup through Twitter. It was also how she got her current job. That gives the question of online status some weight. When the people who might fund your work or hire you are on the same platform, being visible there can have very material consequences.

Someone suggested being on X made you a superior human. Someone else thought it might make you worse. We got from San Francisco’s Twitter following to LA’s Instagram following, with an OnlyFans aside along the way. We were having a very online conversation in very little clothing.

The party was thrown by Afterglow, the peptide company, @afterglow_sci, with Soup. Alchemy Springs was the venue. Afterglow called the event Experiment 02: Body Work. Their invitation proposed a world where thermal spas become the new nightclub, with saunas among friends taking the place of beers at a bar.

Afterglow sells wellness products, including dissolving strips and gummies. Here was the more sociable version of the pitch: an elixir bar, food, music, heat and cold, enough time to actually talk to somebody. The custom peptide blends were on the invitation. I was mostly enjoying the gathering.

I loved how small and relaxing the gathering felt. I had on a black swimsuit and a yellow towel, my hair piled up. In the garden, people stood talking beneath string lights, plants around them and food laid out on a table. It was quiet and chill enough to stay with a conversation.

In the host’s photographs, you can see the Afterglow display and the listening space. Afterglow, @afterglow_sci, and Soup, @secretsoupco, had found a good setting for a conversation with nowhere urgent to go.

Alchemy gave the evening several places to go. There were sofas and paintings, a little tent in the lounge, a DJ at the decks with records behind them. A doorway glowed purple, with red light beyond it. The invitation offered the sauna and cold plunge, a non-alcoholic elixir bar and a listening lounge. Five to seven was for relaxing and charcuterie; seven to nine promised a change in mood.

The venue has its own social ambition. Alchemy’s vision places bathing and time with friends at the center of an evening out. It is a physical place for the kinds of encounters that an online community can set in motion. You can know someone’s handle before you have ever stood beside them in a garden.

With Amy, Atlas, @creatine_cycle, and Nalin, @lordspline, the conversation moved through the power of the platform and the hierarchy that forms around it. Follower counts came up, along with the comparison between San Francisco’s Twitter following and LA’s Instagram following. The platform where your community gathers becomes part of how that community sees you.

David Kanter, @TheKanter, was there too. He co-founded MLCommons and now leads MLPerf, its machine-learning benchmark effort.

Nalin co-founded Capy, which builds cloud coding agents. His feed gives the town-square idea a very concrete next address. In his November 4 post, he invites builders to the Consumer Mobile Hackathon at the YC office on November 15, presented by Capy, Revyl, Convex and Candle. Applications are due November 13. Here is someone from our conversation using the platform to bring another room together, this time around making mobile apps.

Nalin’s November 4 invitation to the Consumer Mobile Hackathon.

Read the original post

Amy had raised money for a startup and found a job through Twitter. The follower-count conversation becomes less abstract when somebody beside you can tell you what being there made possible.

You can meet somebody’s work before meeting them. Or their jokes. Or a tremendous argument about whether they should have been let into a party.

The house-party dispute was part of our conversation too: someone not being let in, and the drama playing out on X. In his original post, Atlas questioned people arriving at a home without an invitation. His follow-up described capacity limits and more requests than he could answer. One phrase in the original stays with the larger conversation: “meet everyone and know no one.”

Atlas on invitations and gathering in San Francisco.

Read the original post · November 1, 2026

A feed makes people familiar in very uneven ways. You know their jokes, the people they reply to, perhaps an oddly detailed account of their week. Then you arrive at a real door, which still belongs to a real person.

I thought Atlas was really cool. He likes posting. I just like posting too.

My dad was in computer engineering, and I’ve always had a computer. I’ve basically always been online. I enjoy the community of it, the conversations, the jokes, the people you keep coming across. I’ve posted nonsense for fun. I still like trolling people on Reddit sometimes.

I’ve had different followings through different stages of social media. But I just like posting. I like making vlogs. I like having my ideas out there. My blog doesn’t even have likes. I put something there, then share it across the other places I use on the internet. The pleasure starts with having something I want to put into the world.

That was what I liked about talking to Atlas. Underneath the hierarchy conversation was someone who enjoyed posting. I recognized that part.

I think we’re heading toward a post-like internet. The counts will keep opening some doors. But I’m interested in what happens when a person finds an idea and thinks: oh, you too.

My blog doesn’t have a little number to put under that encounter. I still want it to happen.

I just like posting. And I want to find the people who understand what I’m putting out there. If I never start sharing it, how are we going to find each other?

I think a post-like internet is coming. Follower counts still open doors. But I just like posting. My blog has no likes. How will like-minded people find us if we never share? A conversation with @amypretzel @creatine_cycle @lordspline @TheKanter.

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

Amy showed me something else she was making, sfrats.com, a map of free and free-ish events around the Bay Area. Music, workshops, markets, comedy. I loved meeting her and seeing an actual project I could explore after the conversation.

Her About page traces the idea back to a free-food club she ran at Stanford, finding campus events with leftover catering. Maddie helps run SF RATS too. It is a practical way of making more of a place available: something is happening, here is where it is, you might want to go.

And the project has already made the trip from website to physical gathering place. In a July 19 post, Amy shows SF RATS events on a tall screen at The Garden, beneath its green neon sign. The list of things to do has become something you can encounter while you are already out in the city. I like that loop: finding a place, arriving, discovering somewhere else to go.

Amy’s July 19 photos of SF RATS events displayed at The Garden.

Read the original post

Met @amypretzel with @creatine_cycle @lordspline @TheKanter at @afterglow_sci’s party. Twitter helped her fund her previous startup and find her current job. She showed me SF RATS, her map of free and free-ish Bay Area events: https://www.sfrats.com/

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

Amy had found work and funding through Twitter. Now she was showing me a website full of places to go. We were already out, in a garden, in towels, making plans through the internet again.

I liked meeting Amy. I liked talking to Atlas. I came home with her website and a conversation I wanted to put somewhere. Apparently I also like posting about liking posting.

title: Giving the idea a body.
deck: Chris had the controller. I had an anime outfit. Dimensional had robots, a disco ball and, eventually, the fire department.
alt: AI-edited editorial outfit portrait of Chloe beside the disco ball
caption: My anime-inspired outfit at Dimensional.
body:
I’m dancing beside the disco ball in a leather jacket, a belted white dress, red tights and black ballet flats. The outfit came from my bedtime anime ritual. I like watching a few anime before I go to sleep, and I’d been watching Smoking Behind the Supermarket with You. She had this cool outfit with a leather jacket over a belted white dress, and I decided to do that for the party. I love dressing like anime.

Chris has a controller in his hands, and there is a robot moving in front of him. Behind him, an enormous American flag takes up the warehouse wall. People stand around watching, holding drinks, talking. The lights keep changing color.

This was our second stop of the night. Dimensional had turned its new Dogpatch facility into an office-warming party. Its name stretched and bent across a wall in purple light. There were sofas, a little goal, a ball on the floor. In my footage, a wheeled, four-legged robot moves through the same space where everyone is hanging out.

I want to translate complex AI technology into visual stories people can follow. At @dimensionalos, my starting point was Chris, a controller and a moving robot in the same frame. A concrete action gives me a way into the technology. @chrisstarrai

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

My first job at a YC company was LivBlends. It was building a machine for making smoothies, and YC’s 2015 founder interview places it in the Summer 2014 batch. Robots have been part of my working life for a long time.

In my archive, there are emails from 2014 where I’m sending the LivBlends team smoothie recipes. Before all this talk of agents and robotics, there I am, trying to help a machine make a better drink.

Found emails from 2014 where I was sending smoothie recipe ideas to LivBlends, my first job at a YC company. Apparently my sales method was already: find something useful to add. I like seeing that thread in my own archive.

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

I want to make complicated AI technology visible. Here, I have a very good starting cast: Chris, a controller and a robot.

Chris looks down at the controls, then up. The robot turns. Someone steps through the frame. A person leans toward it. My phone follows, sometimes a little late. Everyone is trying to get a look.

What does “agentic robotics” actually mean? An AI agent is software that can choose steps toward a goal and use tools to carry them out. In robotics, those tools can help a machine find its way or move an object. The physical action still depends on sensors, motors and control software.

There are several things inside that one movement:

  • The body: wheels, legs, motors and sensors. These give the robot ways to measure its surroundings and move.
  • The movement controls: software that turns a command into coordinated motor movements. A person can give the command with a controller, as Chris does here.
  • The AI agent: software that can choose what to try next, using the tools the developers have connected to it. What it can do depends on those tools and the particular robot.

Dimensional hosted the party and builds dimOS. It’s an open-source set of software tools for connecting those parts: getting information from sensors, keeping track of space and sending commands to a robot. Developers can inspect and change the code. (Dimensional, dimOS source, event invitation)

I also photographed a QR code on one of the robots. Following it gives the machine a name: Gogo. It leads to Houdini’s own Gogo page, which identifies it as a K9 security robot. That little square opens another part of the story. Someone has to turn a robot that moves into a service another person can actually use.

A few names to put with the machines:

  • Houmanoids runs robot services. Its Houdini platform helps organize jobs such as patrols and inspections. The company says it partners with Dimensional on autonomy. My QR photo leads to its page for a robot named Gogo. (Houmanoids, Houdini)
  • DEEP Robotics makes robot bodies. Its wheel-and-leg designs can roll on suitable surfaces and use their legs over uneven ground. Its LYNX M20 family is designed for industrial work, including inspections. Another attendee’s photo shows DEEP branding on the wheeled robots at this party; the exact model variant remains unconfirmed. (Manufacturer’s explanation, Paramendra’s original photo)
  • Unitree also makes robot bodies. The humanoid in my footage looks like its G1, but I haven’t confirmed that identification. A humanoid is a robot with a roughly human-shaped body. Its shape alone doesn’t tell us how independently it can act. (Unitree G1)

Making the hardware, connecting its software and operating it for a customer are different jobs. A machine being at the party does not mean its manufacturer’s team was there too.

To see how the software fits together, imagine asking a suitably equipped robot to go to a doorway. This is an explanatory example, not a task I watched it complete at the party:

  • Find out what’s nearby. Cameras supply pictures. Distance sensors measure how far away surfaces are.
  • Work out where to go. Software uses those readings to estimate the robot’s position and a path toward the doorway.
  • Choose and send an action. An AI agent could request a navigation tool. That tool handles more specific movement instructions.
  • Move and check again. The robot’s controls operate its motors. New sensor readings let the navigation system update its path as conditions change.

Dimensional provides tools for parts of this process, including sensor data, mapping, navigation and remote control. Which parts work on a particular machine depends on its hardware and setup. (Sensor tools, navigation interface, remote control)

In this scene, Chris has the controller. I can see him directing the robot. To call the move autonomous, I would need to know what chose it. The robot is giving a good performance; the footage cannot answer every question about its internal life.

Away from the disco ball, Dimensional has been testing what agents can do with robot tools.

Dimensional’s Can Agents Manipulate?, by Dan B.W. Choe, Ruthwik Dasyam and Sundhar Vinodh Sangeetha, asks a practical question: does giving an AI agent useful robot tools help it complete a physical task?

  • The jobs: lift a bin, remove a bottle cap and arrange letter blocks.
  • The comparison: agents using dimOS tools versus agents using a more basic robot interface.
  • The scale: 900 runs in simulation, meaning a computer-generated test environment. The physical robot comparison was much smaller: one run per setup for each of two tasks.
  • The finding: the authors report faster first successes with dimOS. The small physical sample leaves substantial uncertainty about how reliably that result carries over to other real-world tasks.

It’s the company’s own study. It helps explain what the team is testing; it doesn’t establish what the party robots were doing. (Original report)

How do you show an AI agent acting in the physical world? Follow the decisions: what the camera sees, what the software locates, what the robot does next. @dimensionalos’s research gives me another view to put beside my party footage.

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

A second study, Can Jev Nav?, tests agents navigating simulated homes. There’s an important catch: they receive a written description of the environment, including information a real robot might not have seen yet. Finding a route when you already have that information is a different challenge from discovering the room as you go. (Study by Stash Pomichter, Ruthwik Dasyam and Henry Ventura)

Then I go back to my recording. Chairs, bodies, colored light, somebody walking between me and the robot. An extremely inconvenient room to represent as a tidy problem. Also the sort of room the machine has to live in.

The evening stays human in my phone. There are photos of Chris beneath the flag. Later I turn the camera toward myself, and he leans into the shot. We end up smiling together beneath the warehouse lights.

My footage from @dimensionalos keeps returning to people: Chris with a controller, someone leaning toward a robot, the two of us squeezing into a selfie. The surrounding humans are part of the story. @chrisstarrai

Chloe Starr on X · November 7, 2026

I followed a QR code from a robot to its name, then followed the research back into the software. My phone had caught the movement. There was considerably more happening behind it.

Then the fire alarms went off. The fire department broke up the party, and the night moved outside. My last recordings have a different kind of flashing light: a fire engine on the street, people leaving, then my red tights and ballet flats as I walk away.

The fire-engine footage closes the film.

So that was the office warming: robots, a disco ball, my bedtime-anime outfit, and the fire department. My last shot is of red tights and black ballet flats walking away.

Event photography: Justin Chen (@ch3njus) and Paramendra Kumar Bhagat (@paramendra), linked beneath their photographs. Personal footage and the Chloe/Chris selfie: Chloe Starr. With Chris Starr, @chrisstarrai. Outside research explains the technology and is separate from what I observed at the party.

body:
Listen to the conversation / 15:36

A scripted, AI-generated conversation using an authorized clone of Chloe’s voice and a synthetic female Ancient Witch. Watch on YouTube ↗

Opening chapter / October 2, 2026 in the Portals chronology. Retrospective written and released November 7, 2026. A scripted conversation drawn from my recorded interviews and archive.

SyncSketch → Unity

Inside the studio

ANCIENT WITCHBefore you were making these AI-assisted films, you were selling software to creative teams. What did you need to understand about them?
CHLOE STARR

At SyncSketch, I was talking with people making films, animation and games. The production mattered. A film team might need a tool for three months. If I reached them near the end of a show, I needed to think about the next production. With games, I needed to start the conversation earlier.

Who needed to see the work? How did feedback move? When could the team try something new? The product only made sense once I knew the production around it.

ANCIENT WITCHYou’ve named Disney, Netflix Animation, Epic Games, Naughty Dog, Skydance and Universal Parks in your account history. Pick apart the work for me. How did you get inside an account before anyone was asking you to sell them something?
CHLOE STARR

At Naughty Dog, I was looking for the person responsible for review. At Skydance, I was speaking with an animator who already knew the product. A senior title was not much help if I had found the wrong conversation.

Someone could love SyncSketch with students and friends while their studio had never bought it. Enthusiasm gave us somewhere to start. There was still a different person to find.

ANCIENT WITCHYou described designing your own way into Naughty Dog. What does the original outreach show?
CHLOE STARR

In May 2021, I wrote looking for the person who managed the review pipeline. I named the other people I had contacted and included a short introductory video. I was asking for the owner of a particular process, rather than sending an introduction to the studio and hoping it found someone.

In my later outreach to mudstack, I used that as an example of getting into a studio without an existing connection. It was work I could bring into another company serving a related buyer.

ANCIENT WITCHStay with Naughty Dog. You didn’t have a warm introduction. What did you actually send, and what were you asking the person to do?
CHLOE STARR

I wrote to Almudena Soria and other people around the studio, naming Aaron Limonick, Matt Neapolitan and Paul Kovar among the people I was contacting. I asked who managed the review pipeline and linked a short introduction to the product.

Could they help me find the right person? Or, after watching the video, were they that person? I was trying to get the conversation to the right desk.

ANCIENT WITCHFinding the right person is the beginning. At Naughty Dog, what nearly killed the deal after the artists wanted it?
CHLOE STARR

Legal and procurement. The people who would use SyncSketch wanted it for the next production. They could see what it would change in their creative pipeline. But wanting the tool was not the same as being able to buy it.

We were bootstrapped, including the legal support. The contract work was slow, and they were considering Frame.io. The people I had built relationships with told me what was happening: the other vendor was getting back to them on legal, and we needed our lawyer to respond or they would not get to use us.

ANCIENT WITCHSo the relationship did more than get you a meeting. What did it let you see?
CHLOE STARR

The users still wanted us. The deal could still go away. That was what the relationship let me hear.

The next thing they needed was our lawyer, not another demonstration.

ANCIENT WITCHUniversal Creative was another long one. Why couldn’t you just close it when the creative team said yes?
CHLOE STARR

They were working with intellectual property for the parks, including visual effects for the attractions. They wanted to use SyncSketch to review that work. But the security requirements were serious. You cannot have that material leak.

When I started, SyncSketch did not have SOC 2. There were penetration-testing requirements too. I could not talk someone out of needing those things. I had to maintain the relationship and return as the product’s security position improved.

ANCIENT WITCHWhat were you doing during the wait, beyond sending another “just checking in” email?
CHLOE STARR

Staying in touch with my contact and being interested in the work itself. I love Harry Potter. The enthusiasm was real. I wanted to understand what they were making, and I kept coming back when we had something relevant to bring to the conversation.

In my recorded account, the deal took more than a year. We had to become a product they could approve. I kept the relationship alive while we got there.

ANCIENT WITCHGive me a deal where understanding the creative work changed what you went back to the product team to ask for.
CHLOE STARR

Raised by Wolves. I loved the subject matter. The team asked whether SyncSketch could handle dailies as well as VFX review. If it could, they wanted to use us.

So I went back to the CTO: could we do the dailies? We did not already have a customer I could point to using it that way. We had to check what was technically possible. The production went on to use it for dailies.

ANCIENT WITCHAnd what did you see in that conversation besides one sale?
CHLOE STARR

I was already thinking about a case study. Here was a real question from a production, something we had to check, then a team using the product in a new way. Another studio might recognize itself in that story.

I liked being close to what people were trying to make. Sometimes the sales conversation was also a little investigation: could the tool do this? Who would know? Could we find out together?

THE PUBLISHED CUSTOMER STORYJuly 2022

Raised by Wolves / From the conversation to production

The official SyncSketch case study describes season two coordinating nearly 3,000 VFX shots with 14 vendors, plus studio stakeholders. These are the production’s scale, not Chloe’s personal output.

Published by SyncSketch · byline: BernhardRead the customer story ↗
ANCIENT WITCHWhat about the person who says, “We already have something, and we are not changing it”? Show me how you handled that.
CHLOE STARR

Jon Cowley at FuseFX said exactly why changing tools was difficult. Shotgun was deeply integrated, including with the business and financial side. He could not see them changing it.

I answered with how SyncSketch connected to Shotgun. I explained reviewing the files through SyncSketch, inviting people with a link, adding material during dailies and collaborating across studios. I linked the Sunrise Productions customer story and mentioned upcoming Epic Games and Frontier Studios case studies.

He was not asking for a new production system. He needed to know whether our review tool could live inside the one he already had.

ANCIENT WITCHAnd Skydance? Before the 125-to-250-seat expansion you describe, what did the first conversations look like?
CHLOE STARR

In September 2020, Sergio Díez del Nozal told me he loved SyncSketch and used it with students and friends. I told him I had tried reaching Skydance and had not heard back.

He knew the product. I still had to find the studio’s review owner and the person who could approve buying it. The seat expansion in my later career account came further along. Relationships acquire different kinds of work as they go.

ANCIENT WITCHAnd once you had someone’s attention, what did you find yourself wanting to build?
CHLOE STARR

In June 2021, Taran Matharu was telling me about MPC’s security protocols and existing review tools. He used SyncSketch and had pointed me toward people there. I was getting a view of the world the product would have to enter.

I thought the presentation was holding us back. Some people saw SyncSketch as a product for schools or smaller studios. We had an introductory video people had already seen. I wanted demonstrations and creator content that could help larger teams understand how it might fit.

I watched Taran’s YouTube work, asked how far ahead he planned his topics, and explored whether an Enterprise package could support him. I wanted to bring Bernhard into the conversation and find a partnership that was useful to both sides.

Chloe → Taran / June 21, 2021

“I really believe in content adding value so I would love if I had more of that kind of content.”
ANCIENT WITCHThen SyncSketch became part of Unity. Why keep that as one chapter?
CHLOE STARR

Because it was the same product and the relationships around it continuing inside a larger company. Unity announced the acquisition in November 2021. It makes more sense to follow the work through that change than to treat the names as unrelated jobs.

The commercial results belong in this chapter too: my career records describe $600K+ in SyncSketch revenue and expanding Skydance from 125 to 250 seats at Unity. One describes revenue; the other describes growing an existing relationship.

Now I’m the one trying to make the film. I get to be the user with a tool that almost does what I need, asking whether something can change. I recognize the conversation from the other side.

FROM MY X ARCHIVEApril 2026

The problem I was building around.

Even the best sellers lose deals when data doesn't talk. Not because they can't execute — because they're forced to guess where to focus. At OM we're building for the moment all that data speaks the same language. The teams that win won't move faster. They'll see clearer.
Chloe Starr · @cloeystarrOriginal post ↗

Archive excerpt from the original export. The original post is currently unavailable to X’s embed service.

2026 / Working with agents

ANCIENT WITCHYou spent years helping people adopt software. What happened when you started building with agents yourself?
CHLOE STARR

In February, I was sending people a tool called Pulse and asking for blunt feedback. The question behind it came straight out of sales: given one goal, which accounts should I focus on right now?

By March, Paul and I were trading messages about Claude and workflows. He asked how to put something into Claude. I wrote, “this is something we both have to learn together.” A few days later, I was telling him you could build n8n workflows with Claude. I had found n8n confusing.

That was the beginning: work I wanted to make, tools I was learning while trying to make it. The archive has very little evidence that I arrived knowing everything.

ANCIENT WITCHWhat can someone actually open now?
CHLOE STARR

The website. The films. The archive search. There are poems and stories I wrote years ago beside work I am making now. With Codex, I have been building ways to find the originals and bring selected material into something someone else can visit.

I can search writing, files, media descriptions and exported conversations, then return to the email or photograph underneath. An old thing becomes available for the next thing. That is much of what I want the creation studio to do.

I bring the material, direct, choose, review. The agents help build it. Sometimes I spend rather longer than expected explaining why the thing they have just made is not the thing I meant.

ANCIENT WITCHWhat have you learned to ask of an agent that you didn’t know to ask at the beginning?
CHLOE STARR

An export finishes. The film is wrong. A picture resembles the narration but nobody performs the action. A voice says all the words and sounds like somebody else. “Done” has become a word I investigate.

We started describing the shot more closely: what is here, what happens, what changes, who needs to stay recognizable. We kept the performances and sound on separate tracks. I wanted to fix a picture without breaking a breath.

And please remember the last correction. My voice, my references, the face I chose, the thing I rejected. I would like tomorrow’s session to begin somewhere beyond the start of today’s.

Check out my latest article: My unique Sales Methodology based on my Creative Writing Major https://t.co/S607vlMdNN via @LinkedIn

— Chloe Starr (@cloeystarr) December 17, 2022

Legwork PRM / Build something another rep can use

ANCIENT WITCHWas this already how you worked before SyncSketch?
CHLOE STARR

At Legwork PRM, I proposed a kit for the reps. In July 2016, I broke it into competitor research, the first appointment, the demo and the close. I wanted to sit through competitor demos and make objection-and-rebuttal sheets so the reps could understand the space.

The demo would start with a needs analysis. What was the practice already using? What did it want to do? The presentation should follow those answers. Sometimes the next step was helping the office manager explain it to the doctor.

Jeff wrote back, “We’re good with the $2k for script development.” I had put a scope around the work, with stages and a kit the next person could use.

RangeMe / A conversation someone carries forward

ANCIENT WITCHAt RangeMe, someone forwarded your pitch to other people in the industry. What had you given him?
CHLOE STARR

In January 2018, I followed up a conversation with Chris Jennings about using RangeMe more proactively. I sent him a supplier story and examples of retailer portals, including Sephora.

My 2019 CV records $28K RV in my first month and $115K in Q4 sales at RangeMe. The forwarded conversation shows the work behind a number: helping someone understand the product well enough to explain it to somebody else.

He forwarded the exchange to the Indie Beauty Expo team and asked about a meeting. He described the platform in his own words, explained why it could be useful for vendors, and introduced me with praise for my communication and persuasion.

He had taken the conversation somewhere I was not in the room. I like finding that moment in the archive.

Chris Jennings / January 4, 2018

“Chloe is intuitive, has excellent communication and soft persuasion skills…”

Indie Hackers / Build through other people

ANCIENT WITCHHow did the same instinct turn into a community program?
CHLOE STARR

I recruited, vetted, onboarded and coached people who wanted to organize Indie Hackers meetups. By November 2019, my career record put the program’s growth at 7 to 62 monthly meetups. I wasn’t personally producing every event. I was helping other people become organizers.

In June 2019, someone forwarded me an announcement for a Berkeley meetup. Jason was named as the organizer. I wrote back, “I started that!”

Someone forwarded me a meetup announcement. I had helped start the program; somebody else was now inviting people in. It was lovely to receive the invitation as news.

mudstack / A founder’s response

ANCIENT WITCHWhen you took that experience to another early company, what did the founders see?
CHLOE STARR

I contacted mudstack before there was a job posted. I knew the creative-software buyer and the problem the team was working on. That led to interviews and an offer.

My career records describe securing 35+ podcast guests in two months. That is a count of guests secured. It was another way to build relationships around people making creative work.

After my employment ended, Jordan wrote a long email about our work together. He described being coached by me, offered to be a reference and attributed the ending to the business’s product maturity and market fit.

Jordan Stevens / December 2022

“In three months time you have dramatically transformed our organization and produced exceptional results.”

More commercial work / The figures in my career records

ANCIENT WITCHWhat else belongs beside those stories?
CHLOE STARR

At Lighthouse360, my 2019 CV records Top New Hire in February 2016 and a 90% demo hold rate. At Legwork, it records 60 calls a day, alongside the work of developing the sales kit.

My later Responsive interview preparation records $90K during my Q3 ramp, 18 stalled opportunities and $87K in revived pipeline. Pipeline is a chance to do business, not money already won. That distinction matters when I describe the work.

Check out my latest article: My Personal Hero's Journey to Sales Leadership https://t.co/cnU4o05eWP via @LinkedIn

— Chloe Starr (@cloeystarr) December 19, 2022

Earlier in the archive / LivBlends

CHLOE STARR

In July 2014, I asked about joining the growth team and offered to bring my business network to it. Two days later I sent nut-free smoothie ideas. My later CV records a 42% sales conversion rate; an April 2015 email describes four to seven meetings a day with CEOs and office managers. Later, I rewrote the sales deck and made marketing photographs with a friend. In the email describing that work, I wrote, “I love making things.”

The work now / Making technology understandable

ANCIENT WITCHYou’ve moved between very different kinds of technology. How do you learn enough to sell something you didn’t already know?
CHLOE STARR

I start by asking the people who know the product the questions a buyer will ask me. Existing customer stories help. In an interview this year, I called it a cheat sheet I could defend. I want to know what will happen when somebody actually tries the thing.

At SyncSketch, that meant understanding how a production was put together, who was reviewing the work, and what could stop a studio from approving the tool. With agents, I am also learning by trying to build the things I want to use. I get to find out where my explanation was clear and where it was not.

ANCIENT WITCHWhat do you want to bring to a team building technology that most people are still trying to understand?
CHLOE STARR

There are studios, dental practices, suppliers and meetup organizers in this archive. Different worlds. I kept wanting to understand what someone was trying to do well enough to bring them something they could use.

Working with agents puts me back at the beginning of that process. I ask, try what comes back, find what is missing. Sometimes I need a clearer request. Sometimes the tool needs to become better.

What can I make? Where does this fit? What should I trust? I want to translate complex technology into the language of a person trying to do something with it. I am that person quite a lot of the time now.

In July 2014, I sent smoothie ideas to a company building a machine to make them. “I love making things,” I wrote later. I found that line in the archive while building all of this. Yes. Still.

About this conversation

This scripted conversation was reconstructed from my recorded interviews, correspondence and original work, then voiced with AI. It is not a live interview recording. Historical performance figures are my own career accounts; pipeline, revenue, guests secured and program growth describe different outcomes.

The chronology places this retrospective before the other Portals chapters. It was created and published on November 7, 2026.

body:
Gabriel Jiménez signed with Nicolás Maduro on television. The New York Times later reported that armed guards had detained him before that appearance, threatening him with El Helicoide, a political prison.

He had opposed the government. Then he helped develop its cryptocurrency. How did he end up in that room?

The founder behind UGLYCASH had made a bet: perhaps technology could give Venezuelans a freedom their government would never willingly grant. He tried to build it inside the government’s own project.

CHLOE STARR · @cloeystarr

Gabriel Jiménez opposed Maduro, then helped develop his government’s cryptocurrency. He thought technology could open the money system from inside. Before UGLYCASH, there was that bet, the threats, and the decision to leave Venezuela.

Chloe Starr · November 13, 2026

The bet

Before the Petro, there was a payroll. In his Epicenter interview, Jiménez describes the difficulty of paying employees who lacked dollar accounts. Crypto offered a way to get money to people who had already done the work. His ambition grew from that problem into a much larger attempt to loosen Venezuela’s financial controls.

He had returned after time in the United States, hoping to help change his country. Working with Maduro was a choice. The government had power to open a route he could not open alone. It also had power over him.

In March 2018, while publicly defending the Petro, he told Associated Press reporter Joshua Goodman:

“This is about providing oxygen to people, not a government.”

Goodman’s report warned that the government stood to benefit first, and perhaps most. The same project Jiménez hoped would open the system could strengthen the people controlling it.

The people holding the door

In his 2020 interview with Scott Melker, Jiménez describes a dispute over the Petro’s white paper and its authorship. He says political police came to his home at six in the morning.

Gabriel’s own account · March 31, 2020

Listen to Gabriel’s original interview with Scott Melker, around 50:00 →

The detention around the launch was a separate episode. The investigation by Nathaniel Popper and Ana Vanessa Herrero describes it and the televised signing afterward. A public signature can look like agreement. The room he could not leave belongs in the picture too.

In April 2019, the Times reports, he sold his Toyota Autana to buy a ticket to the United States. A car became a way out of the country.

Leaving did not undo his choice to work on the Petro. Nor does that choice explain away what happened to him afterward. Both stay in the story when he begins building again.

What he makes of it now

UGLYCASH is a later, distinct project. Today its X profile describes an app for “people who make money on the internet.” Creators, freelancers and people working across borders are part of the audience. That brings us back to the original payroll problem: the internet lets you work with someone far away, and getting paid can still be difficult.

GABRIEL JIMÉNEZ · @stablecoinapp · MARCH 19, 2026

“everyone around the world has the same level of access.”

Gabriel’s statement of ambition for UGLYCASH

The company has built a public world around that promise. Its manifesto film moves through blocked opportunities, migration and the difficulty of receiving money from an employer in another country. Its short film about Gabriel gives us a more personal self-portrait: an ambitious man describing vulnerability, mistakes and purpose. In that film, he says, “I’m driven by humanity.”

It is a lot to ask of an app. I wanted to follow the promise out of the founder’s film and into somebody else’s day.

The world between the app and the street

In a recorded design conversation, Gabriel sits with Carlo Santi and Tristen Lerma. He talks about artistic work coming through a person’s “surroundings,” “context” and “experiences.” Santi then shows how objects, stickers and street photography move into the brand and interface. Lerma talks about finding a visual language the internet already speaks.

CHLOE STARR · @cloeystarr

In a UGLYCASH design talk, Gabriel Jiménez says our surroundings and experiences shape what we make. I want to put that beside his history in Venezuela, then look at the choices he makes now. What does that experience change about the product?

Chloe Starr · November 13, 2026

Then there’s the table photograph: patches, cameras, people talking. A financial product has acquired all this physical stuff around it. People are making a place to belong to.

On X, Gabriel had already asked for a physical magazine made from things saved online to be brought into the UGLYCASH space. That movement between a screen and a room shows up in his own feed, too.

GABRIEL JIMÉNEZ · @stablecoinapp · AUGUST 19, 2026

“We need one of those at our @UGLYCASH space”

Gabriel on bringing Offprint into the space

There is a more interesting answer to the design talk on X. Punkable, @0xPunki, a design engineer and creator, describes asking for the company’s poster files during a live broadcast. He then took the posters to a moai and Estadio La Portada in La Serena, Chile, before putting them on his wall.

SOURCE X POST · @0xPunki · August 10, 2026

“Uglycash on my wallet, Uglycash on my wall.”

Read the original post by @0xPunki

Gabriel replied, “this is sooooo awesome”. The posters had made it from the studio to a moai in Chile and back into his replies. Someone had asked for the files and gone on an outing with them.

Punkable’s post includes a referral link. It is an enthusiastic, commercially linked creator account, not independent verification of product claims.

CHLOE STARR · @cloeystarr

A creator asked UGLYCASH for its poster files, took them around La Serena, Chile, and put them on his wall. Gabriel responded on X. I like this little exchange: someone takes the thing you made somewhere you could not have put it yourself.

Chloe Starr · November 13, 2026

From a manifesto to ten minutes

The next voice makes the scale smaller. In a company-published portrait, Luisa Bueso introduces herself as a virtual assistant working from home. She describes moving money and getting an errand down from three hours to ten minutes. The English captions read: “For me, time is extremely valuable.”

Three hours to ten minutes. There is the big promise, suddenly small enough to fit into a working day. What would she rather do with the other two hours and fifty minutes?

CHLOE STARR · @cloeystarr

UGLYCASH’s manifesto talks about global financial access. In a company-published portrait, remote worker Luisa Bueso talks about getting an errand down from three hours to ten minutes. I want those two scales in the same conversation.

Chloe Starr · November 13, 2026

The invitation

We popped into UGLYCASH’s new space on November 11 and 12, including after a trip to the Casper store. Ava Gigantino had invited us to their Better Money Dinner Series.

Her Instagram calls her a vibe curator. Her own introduction to the job adds fundraising, strategic initiatives and operations. She writes that “most opportunities don’t come from a perfect plan,” then describes conversations and introductions. Her invitation to us is one small, actual instance of that work.

AVA GIGANTINO · @avagigantino · OCTOBER 29, 2026
UGLYCASH Studios phase 1 ✔️ · Ava Gigantino

There is a long way from the Petro’s televised signing to Ava inviting us into this space. Designers, filmmakers, people putting posters on Chilean walls, people trying to get paid for their work. A founder can start the story. Other people keep entering it.

We popped in after the Casper store. Gabriel had come by a rather different route. I’m rooting for what they make here.
